opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated ways to look at where we are. We tend to measure progress with things that are hard for humans: olympiad math, bar exams, competitive coding. Models have gotten remarkably good at those. But if you take abilities a young child has, like counting objects in a cluttered scene, telling which of two lines is longer, tracing a path through a simple maze, or understanding how things are arranged in space, today's multimodal models still stumble surprisingly often.

That gap tells you something important. These skills come so naturally to people that we barely think of them as intelligence, yet they sit underneath a lot of what we do: reading a chart, assembling furniture, navigating a room, interpreting a diagram in a scientific paper. If a model can write an essay about geometry but can't reliably tell whether two shapes are touching, it's missing a foundation that general intelligence needs.

So I see basic visual tasks as a kind of reality check. They're cheap to build, easy to verify, and hard to game, because they don't depend on knowledge the model could have memorized from the internet. They test perception and reasoning directly. Tracking how models improve on them gives you a cleaner signal of whether we're actually building more general capabilities, or just getting better at pattern-matching on the text-heavy benchmarks we've been optimizing for.

There's also a broader lesson here. AGI isn't only about reaching the ceiling of human expertise. It's also about covering the floor, the everyday competence any person has. Until models are robust at those basic abilities, especially vision and spatial understanding, I'd be cautious about claiming we're close. In a way, these simple tasks may be among the most honest measures we have.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it is that vision is one of the clearest places where you can see the gap between what a model appears to know and what it actually understands. Language is tricky because a model can sound smart by pattern-matching on text, and it's hard to tell whether there's real comprehension behind it. But with basic visual abilities, there's no hiding. Either you can count the objects in a scene or you can't. Either you can tell that this cup is behind that book, or you can't.

And what's striking is that these are things a three-year-old does effortlessly. Depth, occlusion, object permanence, counting a handful of items, judging whether two shapes are the same, tracking which thing moved where. These aren't skills that require an education or a huge amount of world knowledge. They're kind of the floor of intelligence. And yet frontier models still stumble on them in ways that would surprise people who only interact with them through text.

So I find them useful as a measurement tool for a couple of reasons. One is that they're hard to game. You can't memorize your way through perception the way you can with trivia or even some reasoning benchmarks. The visual world is combinatorially huge, so a model that does well is probably doing something closer to actual understanding. The second is that they're grounded. The answer is checkable against reality, not against a human rater's opinion. That makes them a much more honest signal.

And then the bigger-picture point is that if you believe AGI means something like being able to operate in the world the way a person can, then perception isn't an optional add-on. A model that can write a beautiful essay but can't tell you how many people are standing in a photo is missing something fundamental. So I'd argue these "easy" visual tasks are actually one of the better proxies we have. If we see models close that gap, where they handle the stuff a toddler handles reliably and robustly, that tells me more about progress toward general intelligence than another few points on a text benchmark.

r002.rationale: It says models stumble on basic visual tasks such as counting objects and tracking movement, but does not identify everyday visually guided tasks such as tying shoelaces or assembling furniture.

r003.rationale: It says reliable mastery of toddler-level visual tasks would be a useful signal of progress toward general intelligence, but does not suggest AGI may be close.

astra-6.text:
I think vision gives us a useful way to make a very abstract question more concrete. Instead of just asking, “Is this model intelligent?” we can ask whether it can do things that people do almost without thinking when they look at the world.

For example, can it tell where one object ends and another begins? Can it follow an object when it briefly disappears behind something? Can it understand how objects relate in space? Recognizing that a picture contains a chair is one thing; understanding whether that chair could fit through a doorway requires more.

The interesting part is whether those abilities generalize. If you change the viewpoint or show an unfamiliar arrangement, does the model still understand what’s happening? That helps distinguish a robust capability from success on familiar examples.

I wouldn’t say that human-level vision alone establishes AGI. But these basic abilities give us concrete milestones, and failures can reveal gaps that aren’t obvious when a model is producing very fluent language.

r001.rationale: It describes basic visual abilities but does not say those abilities are roughly similar across most people.

r002.rationale: It gives examples such as object separation and tracking, but does not identify everyday visually guided tasks like tying shoelaces or assembling furniture as abilities current models lack.

r003.rationale: It calls basic visual abilities concrete milestones, but does not suggest that mastering them would mean AGI may be close.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision is a useful way to make the question of progress toward AGI more concrete. People can look at an unfamiliar scene and immediately understand a lot: which objects are there, how they relate to each other, and what might happen next. We take those abilities for granted, but they require more than recognizing patterns or assigning labels.

For example, if you see a cup near the edge of a table, you can reason about whether it might fall and what would happen if someone moved the table. A model might correctly identify the cup and the table while still failing to understand that relationship. So we should test spatial understanding, physical reasoning, and whether those abilities transfer to situations the model hasn’t encountered before.

I wouldn’t say that passing visual tests establishes AGI. But basic human visual abilities give us a useful set of milestones. They help us ask whether a model has developed a general understanding of the world, and they expose gaps that impressive performance on language tasks alone might hide.

r003.rationale: It calls visual abilities useful milestones and says they help assess general world understanding, but does not suggest that mastering them means AGI may be close.
